title: A mosque founded on piety
hook: a mosque founded on mindfulness from the first day, with people who love to be clean (9:108)

segments.voice: Yesterday, awliya', believing men and women at each other's side, and your line was protectors of each other. Whose good point did you make sure got heard? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Two buildings, a few miles apart, both with a place to pray. From the street, you couldn't tell them apart. Same mud brick, same palm trunks, same direction for the prayer. One was built, the Qur'an says, to cause harm, to split the believers and to give cover to someone working against them. The other was built on something you can't see in the brickwork at all. At-Tawbah tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ never to stand in the first one. And it points to the second, with a phrase about foundations that people have carried ever since.
screen: `ONE BUILT ON WHAT YOU CAN'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred seven describes a mosque set up to do damage and to divide; tradition calls it Masjid ad-Dirar, the mosque of harm. Verse one hundred eight says, in paraphrase: never stand in it. A mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in. In it are people who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves. Taqwa is the word Pickthall often renders as duty to God, and others as piety or mindfulness: a constant awareness of God that shapes what you do. So a building can have a foundation under the foundation. Which mosque is meant? Many commentators say Quba, the first mosque of the hijra, which the Prophet helped build with his own hands when he reached the edge of Medina, just after the journey that began in the cave. A hadith in Muslim's collection has the Prophet naming his own mosque in Medina. Scholars have held both, and some say the verse fits both. Then the cleanliness. Commentators connect the people who love to purify themselves with the people of Quba, who were known for washing carefully with water. A hadith reported by Ibn Majah and an-Nasa'i says that whoever purifies himself at home, then comes to Quba and prays there, has a reward like a lesser pilgrimage. Inner and outer meet in one verse: a heart that's honest about why it built something, and hands that keep the place clean. Neither is an extra. The intention is the foundation; the cleaning is how you live in the house.
screen: `THE MOSQUE OF HARM.` · `TAQWA FROM THE FIRST DAY.` · `QUBA, OR THE PROPHET'S MOSQUE.` · `PEOPLE WHO LOVE TO BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `FOUNDED ON PIETY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean a shared space. First, sit, and think of a place you share with other people. A kitchen, an office, a break room, a prayer room, a stairwell. Picture the corner of it nobody takes care of. Ask yourself one quiet question, the verse's question: why do I do the things I do there? When the bell ends, you can go and clean that one corner, without telling anyone. If you pray, you can begin it with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
A mosque founded on piety. A place built from the first day on taqwa, awareness of God, and kept by people who love to be clean. Today's word.
screen: `A MOSQUE FOUNDED ON PIETY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: founded on piety. Today, before you start one thing, a project, a message, a plan, check the foundation: why am I building this? Day four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many visitors to Medina pray at the Quba mosque, often after making wudu first, following the hadith on its reward; volunteers in mosques around the world take turns cleaning the prayer hall and the washing area.

pairs: the mosque built to cause harm
the first mosque of the hijra

myth: the verse names the mosque founded on piety
it doesn't. many say Quba; a hadith in Muslim names the Prophet's mosque; some say both.
the mosque of harm looked like any other mosque
the difference the verse names is the intention under the bricks.
cleanliness is mentioned in the same verse as piety
God loves those who purify themselves, right after the foundation of taqwa.

fork.setup: a group invites the Prophet to pray in their new mosque. it looks like any other. what does the Qur'an tell him?
options: pray there once, to keep the peace.
pray there, but don't stay long.
fork.reveal: never stand in it: it was built to cause harm and division. a mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy.

original.note: Arabic: piety, mindfulness, awareness of God; the foundation the verse names (9:108).

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse about choosing the right mosque.
what it means: a building's real foundation is the intention under it, and the people who keep it clean.
what a scholar hears: commentators debate whether the mosque is Quba or the Prophet's mosque in Medina (Sahih Muslim names the latter); the purifiers are linked to the people of Quba.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1398 (the mosque founded on taqwa is the Prophet's mosque)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1412; Sunan an-Nasa'i 699 (purifying at home and praying at Quba)

notes: 9:107–108 paraphrased rather than quoted. Confirm the paraphrase.
Hadith numbers (Muslim 1398; Ibn Majah 1412; Nasa'i 699) cited from memory; confirm, and confirm the Quba reward hadith's grading.
The link between 'men who love to purify themselves' and the people of Quba washing with water is from tafsir reports (e.g. Abu Dawud 44); confirm the wording 'commentators connect'.
Claim that the Prophet helped build Quba with his own hands on arriving at Medina: sira tradition; confirm.
